title: Remote Web Task Recipes
user: A low-vision or screen-reader user who must complete recurring tasks in browser-delivered remote/legacy software that exposes little usable accessibility metadata.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says accessibility APIs only work where supported and describes remote or unusual employer software as a practical barrier to accessible work.
A VS Code feature request asks to replace a static Accessible View with an integrated, scrollable and copyable view for screen-reader users.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 requests in work software; failure blocks a user from completing ordinary navigation and review tasks, not merely a preference.
current_workaround: Zoom everything, memorize click locations, ask a colleague, or switch between a screen reader and a visual remote-desktop view.
incumbents_and_gap: NVDA, VoiceOver and Windows Magnifier are essential general tools, but they cannot add task-specific landmarks to a browser canvas or remote application that exposes no semantics.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension where a user or support worker records named, keyboard-reachable visual landmarks for one browser app and attaches concise spoken task steps. It uses user-triggered tab screenshots/OCR only to help place landmarks. Non-goals: remote-control automation, credential capture, employer surveillance, or an AI agent that clicks for the user.
success_measure: In a five-task pilot, a participant completes at least four recurring tasks without sighted assistance after creating no more than ten landmarks.
monetization: one-time — a local accessibility accommodation should remain useful without a recurring data fee.
constraints: Process screenshots locally; never upload page pixels or DOM text by default; encrypt exported recipes; require a deliberate user gesture before capture; do not claim compatibility with every remote desktop.
why_distinct: It supplies reusable, user-owned task landmarks in inaccessible browser surfaces rather than trying to replace a screen reader or automate employment decisions.

title: TapRead Canvas
user: An Android user who needs text in a game, streamed desktop, image, or custom canvas read aloud quickly without waiting for the app to implement accessibility labels.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer who could not play PC games on Linux describes building a GPU-accelerated select-to-speak overlay because conventional readers could not read text in games or video.
The request for a dedicated NVDA/JAWS screen-reader mode demonstrates that text-heavy tools still need an accessibility-specific interaction path.

recurrence: Two independent accessibility requests in 2025–26; canvas and non-semantic text turn a usable device into an inaccessible one.
current_workaround: Use system Select to Speak where it works, take screenshots into an OCR app, ask someone else, or abandon the activity.
incumbents_and_gap: Android Select to Speak, Lookout and TalkBack help in supported contexts; none makes a fast, privacy-preserving rectangular OCR-and-speech action for arbitrary on-screen canvas text the focused workflow.
smallest_useful_product: An Android accessibility-service companion: a user invokes a floating button, draws one rectangle, gets on-device OCR and immediate TTS, and can repeat the last region. Non-goals: continuous screen recording, gameplay automation, remote streaming, translation, or cloud OCR.
success_measure: At least 80% of 30 user-selected regions are correctly read aloud within two seconds on mid-range hardware, with no network request.
monetization: one-time — on-device assistive utility value is direct and should not be metered by pages read.
constraints: Android accessibility-service disclosure and Play policy compliance; all OCR/TTS local; clear warning around sensitive screens; do not bypass DRM or protected-content controls.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately narrow, one-gesture reading aid for inaccessible pixels, not another general OCR scanner or voice assistant.

title: Caption Lens
user: A hard-of-hearing person at an event, talk, or shared video who needs personal, readable live captions without requiring everyone else to turn captions on.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker proposes movie-theater captions visible only through special glasses, seeking a way to make captions personal rather than disruptive to others.
A feature request for real-time captions cites hard-of-hearing users in a diverse social/virtual community.

recurrence: Two independent caption-access requests across physical and virtual shared experiences; missing speech excludes participation in real time.
current_workaround: Rely on venue equipment, lip-read, use the platform's small/default captions, or ask a companion for repeats.
incumbents_and_gap: Live Transcribe, iOS Live Captions, Ava and platform captions exist; the gap is a disposable personal display with huge type, contrast controls, line hold, and no account or meeting-bot setup.
smallest_useful_product: An offline-first PWA that transcribes microphone input on-device where supported, renders one high-contrast caption line with adjustable hold/size, and offers a manual correction keypad. Non-goals: recording a meeting, identifying speakers, translation, medical claims, or venue-system integration.
success_measure: In a controlled conversation, users can keep caption text legible at their chosen distance and rate it usable in at least 8 of 10 five-minute sessions.
monetization: free — a no-account utility is important for spontaneous access; optional one-time native packaging can follow.
constraints: Make on-device processing status unmistakable; microphone permission only while active; do not retain audio/transcripts; accuracy varies by device, noise and language.
why_distinct: The product is a personal caption display optimized for legibility and dignity, not a meeting recorder or generic transcription SaaS.

title: Caption Cues
user: A viewer with high-frequency hearing loss who can follow captions but needs the most easily misheard names, words, and sound cues to stand out.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker specifically requests bold caption styling for words likely to be misheard, with settings for different hearing-loss profiles.
A caption-settings request distinguishes dialogue-only subtitles from full captions, showing that a single caption toggle cannot satisfy different needs.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 requests for more meaningful caption controls; default captions are present but insufficiently adaptable.
current_workaround: Replay a scene, increase all caption text, turn on every sound-description cue, or manually switch among poorly named subtitle options.
incumbents_and_gap: Netflix and browser players expose caption size and style, while subtitle extensions mainly restyle everything. They rarely add a viewer-controlled hierarchy for proper names, uncertain words, speaker changes and sound cues.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that transforms captions already exposed by the page: selectable emphasis rules for names, speaker changes, bracketed sound cues and manually saved words; keyboard replay of the last line. Non-goals: generating captions, scraping protected streams, diagnosing hearing loss, or claiming clinical personalization.
success_measure: In a 20-minute test video, participants request replay for at least 30% fewer lines than with their player’s ordinary caption styling.
monetization: one-time — the extension works locally against captions the user already has access to.
constraints: Only operate on caption DOM/tracks available to the user; no video download or DRM circumvention; rules are assistive preferences, not medical recommendations.
why_distinct: It improves comprehension within existing captions instead of offering another caption generator or a blanket font/theme switcher.

title: Transcript Study View
user: A person who absorbs text better than video or audio and wants a calm, navigable reading version of a talk they are already watching.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says text is easier to absorb than audio/video and asks for a way to obtain and read TED/YouTube transcripts without broken lines and repeated copy-paste.
A text-to-speech output request explicitly frames listening to long responses as both an accessibility aid and a multitasking workflow.

recurrence: Two independent requests show that people switch between listening and reading rather than treating one modality as universally accessible.
current_workaround: Open a platform transcript panel, copy it into a document, use reader mode, or rely on auto-transcripts with awkward line breaks.
incumbents_and_gap: YouTube/TED transcript panels, Reader Mode and Speechify cover pieces; there is no lightweight view that preserves timestamps while making source-provided transcript text genuinely skimmable and reversible to audio.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that detects an official transcript/caption track visible to the user and opens a local reader with paragraphs, timestamp jump links, dyslexia-friendly spacing and optional browser TTS. Non-goals: downloading media, transcribing unavailable content, hiding attribution, summaries, or LLM rewriting.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot users finish a selected 10-minute talk using the transcript view and use three or more timestamp jumps or saved highlights.
monetization: free — it needs broad compatibility and trust; a paid export pack would be optional later.
constraints: Use only text/caption tracks the site exposes to the signed-in user; preserve source URL and timestamps; no copyrighted media download or anti-bot bypass; local highlights by default.
why_distinct: It is a modality-switching reading surface for existing transcripts, not a content summarizer or video downloader.

title: Caption Source Check
user: A viewer or event volunteer who needs to know whether a live stream has an official usable caption track and a clean way to follow that track outside a cluttered player.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants a simple live-updated transcript for NASA communications and reports that obtaining the existing high-quality YouTube subtitles is difficult.
A transcript feature request identifies missing captions as a failure case and asks for a local fallback, evidence that caption availability is still unreliable.

recurrence: Two 2026 transcript requests show a recurring availability and readability problem around live captions, not a shortage of video players.
current_workaround: Dig through player menus, try fragile downloader scripts, or give up when a stream’s caption UI fails.
incumbents_and_gap: YouTube captions, yt-dlp and transcript services each solve part of the path but combine policy risk, brittle extraction, or an overwhelming video interface. A clear availability check is missing.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that reports whether the current page exposes an official caption track, its language/type and live status, then presents that user-visible track in a simple large-text pane. Non-goals: extracting hidden tracks, downloading video/audio, Whisper fallback, DRM bypass or defeating site restrictions.
success_measure: On a test set of 50 public streams, it correctly reports exposed-caption availability and language at least 95% of the time.
monetization: free — transparent availability information is a public-good utility and avoids incentives to bypass platforms.
constraints: Read only page/player data the browser already makes available; comply with host terms; no content retention; clearly distinguish machine-generated from human captions when metadata exists.
why_distinct: It deliberately stops short of extraction or transcription and makes the official captions a dependable accessibility signal.

title: Workspace Profiles
user: A knowledge worker with declining vision who needs Office, docs, dashboards and browser apps to become readable without losing context every time zoom changes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A knowledge worker with worsening eyesight asks which tools can help across Office 365, Teams, Google Docs, Confluence, Salesforce and PowerBI.
A low-vision user says uniform built-in zoom is uncomfortable and asks for font scaling and UI customization rather than one scale for the whole interface.

recurrence: Two independent work-software requests; uniform zoom sacrifices either context or readable text across the tools needed for a job.
current_workaround: Use browser zoom, OS magnification, inverted contrast and large fonts, then repeatedly reconfigure sites and lose layout context.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser zoom, Windows Magnifier, macOS Zoom and extensions such as Zoom Page WE are broad controls; they do not save per-workspace profiles that enlarge body text while preserving critical navigation and data-table density.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension with named profiles per domain: independent text scale, line spacing, contrast, cursor halo and a hotkey to temporarily magnify the focused region. Non-goals: changing employer documents, remote-desktop capture, screen-reader replacement or collecting browsing analytics.
success_measure: After one week, a pilot user activates saved profiles on three or more work sites and reports fewer than one manual zoom reset per site/day.
monetization: one-time — accessible personal settings should stay local and usable even if a service closes.
constraints: Keep profiles on device; respect site CSP and avoid injecting into password/payment fields by default; test keyboard focus and reflow so added styling does not create new barriers.
why_distinct: It treats readable work as a profile of several reversible controls rather than assuming that enlarging every pixel is enough.

title: Color Meaning Lens
user: A color-blind technical worker who needs status, diffs and charts to convey their meaning without depending on red, green or yellow alone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A technical user asks how people deal with color blindness on screens and says OS/game correction options do not cover the full spectrum.
A Codex user reports that code diffs are not accessible for people with red-green color blindness.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 technical-work requests; color-only status can hide errors and change review outcomes.
current_workaround: Use system color filters, memorize position, inspect raw text, buy color-filter glasses, or avoid visual QA work.
incumbents_and_gap: OS color filters and color-blind simulators transform pixels globally, while GitHub-style products fix only their own UI. Users lack a reversible browser overlay that adds textual/shape meaning to familiar state colors.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that lets users map page colors to patterns and short labels (for example PASS, WARN, FAIL), with a per-site eyedropper and keyboard toggle. Non-goals: medical color correction, claiming to identify every semantic color, altering source data, or image editing.
success_measure: For a seeded dashboard/diff task, participants correctly classify at least 90% of color-coded states with the lens enabled versus their baseline.
monetization: one-time — the value is personal configuration and no hosted color data is needed.
constraints: All mappings local; preserve text contrast and focus indicators; avoid reading pixels from cross-origin canvases without a user action; labels must remain removable and not be presented as ground truth.
why_distinct: It overlays semantic redundancy at the point of use instead of applying a one-size-fits-all color filter.

title: Form Guard
user: A dyslexic user completing high-stakes web forms who wants to catch avoidable transpositions and ambiguous typed labels before submission without surrendering form data to a service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A dyslexic programmer explains that stressful situations place heavy demands on working memory and describes relying on notes, tools and time to process information.
A feature request written from a dyslexic user’s perspective asks to enter a number rather than spell a region name in order to avoid typos.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 accounts connect dyslexia with error-prone typed labels and high working-memory demand, especially when mistakes are costly.
current_workaround: Proofread repeatedly, copy known values from elsewhere, use generic spellcheck, or ask another person to check a form.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser spellcheck catches dictionary errors and password managers fill known fields; neither makes a privacy-preserving, opt-in final review of likely transpositions, duplicate words and field/value mismatches across arbitrary forms.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension invoked before submit that reads visible editable fields aloud/on screen, flags repeated words, adjacent transpositions and inconsistent retyped values, and offers a one-field-at-a-time review mode. Non-goals: automatic form submission, credit/identity decisions, cloud spell correction or diagnosing dyslexia.
success_measure: In a seeded form set, users catch at least 70% of intended transposition/duplicate errors while generating no more than one false alert per form.
monetization: one-time — users should not have to upload sensitive form text for ongoing proofreading.
constraints: Local-only analysis; disable by default on password, banking, health and government domains; never persist field values; accessibility review must not make invalid claims about medical benefit.
why_distinct: It is a controlled last-mile form review, not a generic grammar checker or an automated decision maker.

title: Reading Rail
user: A reader with dyslexia or visual crowding who needs to keep their place in dense browser text and review one manageable line or paragraph at a time.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN discussion about a colleague's frequent typos notes that errors escape ordinary spell-checking and are caught late, reflecting a need for better error-prevention supports.
A request says dyslexia-friendly fonts in a web app are hard to find, indicating that merely shipping a font setting does not make a reading aid usable.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 discussions around dyslexia-related reading/writing friction; defaults and buried settings do not prevent errors.
current_workaround: Change the whole page font, use a physical ruler, copy text to another app, or rely on a generic reader mode that loses the original context.
incumbents_and_gap: OpenDyslexic fonts, browser reader modes and BeeLineReader offer useful alternatives, but many are font-first or rewrite the page. The gap is a keyboard-first, reversible focus rail that works in-place.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension with a movable focus rail, dimmable surrounding paragraphs, per-site line-height/letter-spacing presets, and optional browser TTS for the current line. Non-goals: special-font claims, page summarization, tracking reading behavior, or medical treatment claims.
success_measure: In a timed proofreading test, users retain their place after an interruption at least 25% more often than with their ordinary browser view.
monetization: free — a simple local reading accommodation benefits from wide access; optional one-time sync/export can follow.
constraints: No content upload or analytics by default; keep native selection, links and screen-reader behavior intact; offer instant escape/reset; test against reflow and WCAG text-spacing requirements.
why_distinct: The primary artifact is an in-place attention guide, not an unproven font or another reader-mode clone.

title: Interview Recall Deck
user: A job seeker with ADHD who needs a low-pressure, repeatable way to prepare and retrieve their own experience examples under interview stress.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An unemployed developer with ADHD says impaired executive function and memory make advance preparation and recall during interviews extremely difficult.
A request explicitly seeks ADHD/dyslexia-friendly developer and focus tooling, including voice-oriented supports and reduced cognitive load.

recurrence: Two independent requests across 2025–26; the harm is missed employment opportunity rather than ordinary productivity friction.
current_workaround: Use generic flashcards, cram notes, ask an LLM to invent answers, or keep scattered documents that are hard to retrieve under pressure.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki, Notion templates and interview-prep services are flexible but demand setup and rarely rehearse retrieval of a user's own evidence in short, accessible chunks.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA that turns a user’s own projects into short prompt/evidence cards, supports a timed but pausable voice-or-text rehearsal, and surfaces a one-page pre-interview recall sheet. Non-goals: generating false experience, diagnosing ADHD, scoring candidates, video surveillance or recruiter integrations.
success_measure: After seven days, at least 60% of pilot users can recall three concrete examples for each chosen competency without consulting full notes.
monetization: one-time — a personal preparation aid has episodic value and should protect sensitive career details locally.
constraints: Local-first encrypted export; explicitly label any optional drafting aid as user-edited; no mental-health claims; accessibility includes keyboard, TTS and reduced-motion controls.
why_distinct: It supports truthful recall of a person’s own work rather than becoming an interview-answer generator or a generic task manager.

title: Next Step Cards
user: A person with executive-function fatigue who needs to resume a real task after interruption without reopening an overwhelming project plan or relying on a chat assistant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A non-engineer asks how people use AI as an external executive function for planning and action while avoiding over-reliance and loss of judgment.
An issue calls for attention-management and executive-function supports that reduce cognitive overhead while completing tasks.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 requests explicitly frame executive function as a workflow support need; dependence on a conversational system is itself a stated concern.
current_workaround: Keep long to-do lists, reopen many tabs, ask an AI what to do next, or abandon the task after an interruption.
incumbents_and_gap: Todoist, Things, Sunsama and AI planners organize many tasks; the unresolved small need is a single deliberate continuation card that records the exact next physical action, context and stop condition.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA with one active card: task name, next 2-minute action, required link/file, why it matters, and a completion/park decision. It can schedule a gentle local reminder and show a re-entry history. Non-goals: LLM planning, social accountability, surveillance, streak pressure or treatment claims.
success_measure: During a two-week pilot, users resume a parked task within five minutes at least 50% more often than their baseline, measured by their own card completions.
monetization: one-time — the utility stores personal context locally and should not require a subscription for basic recall.
constraints: No dark patterns, streaks or guilt notifications; all data local/exportable; reminders must respect OS quiet hours and reduced-motion preferences; do not present as clinical support.
why_distinct: It minimizes the re-entry decision to one user-authored next action instead of becoming another AI coach or expansive productivity system.
